activities.title: The four numbers that gate every AIF scheme

payload.hook: Before strategy, before category, four numbers decide whether a scheme can exist at all: corpus, ticket size, investor count and the form units take. Get one wrong and the scheme is defective from launch.

cards.title: Twenty crore a scheme
cards.law: Each scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have corpus of at least twenty crore rupees; each scheme of a social impact fund shall have a corpus of at least five crore rupees.
cards.means: The floor attaches to each SCHEME, not to the fund as a whole. A fund running three schemes must clear it three times.
cards.watch: The five-crore concession is confined to social impact funds. It is not a small-fund exemption.
cards.link: Pairs with the ticket-size rule below.

cards.title: One crore, with two carve-outs
cards.law: The AIF shall not accept from an investor an investment of value less than one crore rupees. Provided that for employees or directors of the AIF or of the Manager, the minimum shall be twenty five lakh rupees. Provided further that this clause shall not apply to an accredited investor.
cards.means: One crore is the general floor; twenty-five lakh for insiders; and the floor does not apply at all to an accredited investor.
cards.watch: The accredited-investor carve-out disapplies the clause entirely — it is not a reduced figure.
cards.link: Accreditation recurs across the regime.

cards.title: One thousand per scheme
cards.law: No scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have more than one thousand investors.
cards.means: A per-scheme ceiling, counted scheme by scheme.
cards.watch: Where the AIF is formed as a company, the Companies Act, 2013 applies in addition.
cards.link: Contrast with the angel fund concentration rule.

cards.title: Units in dematerialised form
cards.law: The Alternative Investment Fund shall issue units in dematerialised form subject to the conditions specified by the Board from time to time.
cards.means: Physical unit certificates are no longer the default position.
cards.watch: Inserted by amendment — a point where older material is out of date.
cards.link: See the amendment tracker.

payload.summary: Four gates per scheme: corpus twenty crore (five crore for a social impact fund); minimum investment one crore, twenty-five lakh for employees and directors, and disapplied entirely for an accredited investor; not more than one thousand investors; and units issued in dematerialised form.
payload.tip: Check the four gates scheme by scheme, not fund by fund. The most common error in structuring is treating corpus and investor count as fund-level tests when the regulation applies them to each scheme.

activities.title: The minimum corpus prescribed for each scheme of an AIF is:

payload.q: The minimum corpus prescribed for each scheme of an AIF is:

options.t: Twenty crore rupees, reduced to five crore for a social impact fund
Twenty crore rupees for the fund as a whole, whatever its schemes
Ten crore rupees per scheme, with no concession for any category
Five crore rupees per scheme, raised to twenty crore for Category III

payload.explanation: Reg. 10(b): each scheme shall have a corpus of at least twenty crore rupees, with the proviso reducing this to five crore for each scheme of a social impact fund. The test is per scheme, not per fund.

answer.explanation: Reg. 10(b): each scheme shall have a corpus of at least twenty crore rupees, with the proviso reducing this to five crore for each scheme of a social impact fund. The test is per scheme, not per fund.

The commitment is permissible, because the minimum does not apply to an accredited investor
The commitment fails, because twenty-five lakh applies only to insiders
The commitment is permissible only if the investor is also a director of the Manager

payload.explanation: The second proviso to Reg. 10(c) disapplies the minimum-investment clause altogether for an accredited investor. It is not a reduced threshold but an exemption from the clause.

The ceiling applies to the fund as a whole, so the scheme has ample headroom

activities.title: Structure and tenure: what your category fixes for you

payload.hook: Category is not just a label for your strategy. It decides whether your fund can be open-ended at all, and how long it may run.

cards.title: Close-ended by category
cards.law: Category I and Category II Alternative Investment Funds shall be close ended and the tenure of the fund or scheme shall be determined at the time of application. Schemes of Category III Alternative Investment Fund may be open ended or close ended.
cards.means: Categories I and II have no open-ended option. Only Category III schemes may choose.
cards.watch: Tenure is fixed at application for Categories I and II — not later.
cards.link: Drives the extension rule.

cards.title: Three years
cards.law: Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds or schemes launched by such funds shall have a minimum tenure of three years.
cards.means: A floor, not a default. Anything shorter cannot be registered.
cards.watch: The three-year floor attaches to Categories I and II; Category III is governed by its chosen structure.

cards.title: Two years, two-thirds
cards.law: Extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund.
cards.means: Up to two years, and only with a two-thirds vote measured by value.
cards.watch: By value, not by number of unit holders. Counting heads is the classic error.
cards.link: Compare the continuing-interest tests, also value-based.

payload.summary: Categories I and II must be close-ended with tenure fixed at application and a minimum of three years; Category III schemes may be open- or close-ended; and a close-ended fund's tenure may be extended by up to two years with the approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value.
payload.tip: Diarise the tenure end date at registration, not at first close. The two-thirds-by-value vote takes time to organise, and an expired tenure cannot be cured retrospectively.

activities.title: A close-ended Category II fund seeks to extend its tenure. The require

payload.q: A close-ended Category II fund seeks to extend its tenure. The requirement is approval of:

options.t: A simple majority of the unit holders, counted by number of holders
Three-fourths of the unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
Two-thirds of the unit holders by number, with the Board's prior approval
Two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the fund

payload.explanation: Reg. 13(5): extension of up to two years requires approval of two-thirds of the unit holders BY VALUE of their investment. The vote is value-weighted, not a headcount.

answer.explanation: Reg. 13(5): extension of up to two years requires approval of two-thirds of the unit holders BY VALUE of their investment. The vote is value-weighted, not a headcount.

activities.title: A sponsor proposes an open-ended Category II fund with a two-year tenu

payload.q: A sponsor proposes an open-ended Category II fund with a two-year tenure. The compliance officer should identify:

options.t: Two defects — Category II must be close-ended and the tenure is below three years
One defect — only the tenure, since Category II funds may be open-ended
One defect — only the structure, since two years is a permissible tenure
No defect, provided the tenure is fixed at the time of the application

payload.explanation: Reg. 13(1) requires Categories I and II to be close-ended, and Reg. 13(2) sets a minimum tenure of three years. Both limbs fail independently — the open-ended option belongs to Category III alone.

answer.explanation: Reg. 13(1) requires Categories I and II to be close-ended, and Reg. 13(2) sets a minimum tenure of three years. Both limbs fail independently — the open-ended option belongs to Category III alone.

activities.title: Which categories may be open-ended, and what is the minimum tenure?

payload.q: Which categories may be open-ended, and what is the minimum tenure?
payload.answer: Only schemes of a Category III AIF may be open- or close-ended. Categories I and II shall be close-ended with tenure determined at the time of application, and a minimum tenure of three years.

answer.answer: Only schemes of a Category III AIF may be open- or close-ended. Categories I and II shall be close-ended with tenure determined at the time of application, and a minimum tenure of three years.

activities.title: Skin in the game: the continuing interest

payload.hook: The regulation makes the Manager or Sponsor put money alongside the investors — and is precise about how much, and how it may not be provided.

cards.title: Lower of two figures
cards.law: Continuing interest in the Alternative Investment Fund of not less than two and half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower, in the form of investment in the Alternative Investment Fund, and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees. Provided that for Category III Alternative Investment Fund, the continuing interest shall be not less than five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower.
cards.means: Categories I and II: 2.5% of corpus or five crore, whichever is LOWER. Category III: 5% or ten crore, whichever is lower.
cards.watch: Whichever is LOWER, not higher. On a large corpus the rupee cap binds, not the percentage.
cards.link: Category III carries double the percentage.

cards.title: Not by waiving fees
cards.law: …and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees.
cards.means: The interest must be a real investment. Foregoing fees does not count.
cards.watch: A fee waiver structured as economic exposure still fails this test.

cards.title: Tell the investors
cards.law: The Manager or Sponsor shall disclose their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund to the investors of the Alternative Investment Fund.
cards.means: Holding the interest is not enough; it must be disclosed to investors.
cards.watch: Disclosure is a separate obligation from the holding itself.

payload.summary: The Manager or Sponsor must hold a continuing interest of not less than 2.5% of corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower (5% or ten crore, whichever is lower, for Category III), by way of actual investment and not through any waiver of management fees, and must disclose that investment to investors.
payload.tip: Compute both limbs at every close, since corpus moves. On a corpus above two hundred crore the rupee cap is what binds for Categories I and II — running the percentage alone will overstate the requirement.

activities.title: For a Category II AIF, the continuing interest of the Manager or Spons

payload.q: For a Category II AIF, the continuing interest of the Manager or Sponsor must be not less than:

options.t: Five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower
Two and a half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower
Two and a half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is higher
Five percent of the corpus, with no monetary cap applying to the figure

payload.explanation: Reg. 10(d): 2.5% of corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is LOWER, for Categories I and II. The 5%/ten crore pair applies to Category III, and the test is the lower of the two, not the higher.

answer.explanation: Reg. 10(d): 2.5% of corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is LOWER, for Categories I and II. The 5%/ten crore pair applies to Category III, and the test is the lower of the two, not the higher.

activities.title: A Category III fund with a corpus of four hundred crore rupees propose

payload.q: A Category III fund with a corpus of four hundred crore rupees proposes to meet its continuing interest by waiving management fees of twelve crore. The defect is that:

options.t: The amount is short, since five percent of four hundred crore is twenty crore
Category III funds are not subject to any continuing interest requirement at all
The interest must be an actual investment and cannot be a waiver of management fees
The waiver is permissible only if disclosed to investors in the placement memorandum

payload.explanation: Two points. The rupee cap means ten crore would satisfy the amount, since the test is the lower of 5% or ten crore. But Reg. 10(d) requires the interest to take the form of investment and expressly excludes a waiver of management fees, so the structure fails on form regardless of quantum.

But Reg. 10(d) requires the interest to take the form of investment and expressly excludes a waiver of management fees, so the structure fails on form regardless of quantum.

activities.title: Category III: leverage, and what it is conditioned on

payload.hook: Category III is the only category that may employ leverage — but the permission is conditional, and the conditions are where compliance actually lives.

cards.title: Leverage, on consent and within a limit
cards.law: Category III Alternative Investment Funds may engage in leverage or borrow subject to consent from the investors in the fund and subject to a maximum limit, as may be specified by the Board.
cards.means: Two conditions attach: investor consent, and a maximum limit specified by the Board.
cards.watch: Consent alone is not enough, and neither is staying under the limit. Both must hold.
cards.link: Contrast the closed structure rules in Module 2.

cards.title: Four things to report
cards.law: Provided that such funds shall disclose information regarding the overall level of leverage employed, the level of leverage arising from borrowing of cash, the level of leverage arising from position held in derivatives or in any complex product, and the main source of leverage in their fund to the investors and to the Board periodically.
cards.means: Overall leverage, cash-borrowing leverage, derivative leverage and the main source — to investors and to the Board.
cards.watch: Aggregate leverage alone does not satisfy this; the composition must be broken out.

cards.title: Regulated by direction
cards.law: Category III Alternative Investment Funds shall be regulated through issuance of directions regarding areas such as operational standards, conduct of business…
cards.means: Much of the Category III regime sits in directions rather than in the regulation text.
cards.watch: Reading the regulation alone will not give you the full Category III picture.
cards.link: See the Master Circular modules.

payload.summary: Category III AIFs may engage in leverage or borrow, but only with investor consent and within a maximum limit specified by the Board, and must periodically disclose overall leverage, leverage from cash borrowing, leverage from derivatives or complex products, and the main source of leverage, both to investors and to the Board.
payload.tip: Treat the leverage disclosure as four separate data points rather than one number. A report showing only aggregate leverage is incomplete on the face of the proviso.

activities.title: A Category III fund obtains investor consent and employs leverage with

payload.q: A Category III fund obtains investor consent and employs leverage within the specified limit, reporting only its overall leverage each quarter. The defect is that:

options.t: Leverage requires the prior approval of the Board in addition to investor consent
Category III funds may not employ leverage arising from derivative positions at all
Reporting is required monthly rather than quarterly for any leveraged Category III fund
The disclosure must break out cash borrowing, derivatives and the main source too

payload.explanation: The proviso to Reg. 17(c) requires disclosure of the overall level of leverage, the level arising from borrowing of cash, the level arising from derivatives or complex products, and the main source — to investors and to the Board. An aggregate figure alone is incomplete.

answer.explanation: The proviso to Reg. 17(c) requires disclosure of the overall level of leverage, the level arising from borrowing of cash, the level arising from derivatives or complex products, and the main source — to investors and to the Board. An aggregate figure alone is incomplete.

activities.title: Leverage by a Category III AIF is permitted subject to:

payload.q: Leverage by a Category III AIF is permitted subject to:

options.t: Consent from the investors and a maximum limit as specified by the Board
The prior written approval of the Board for each borrowing transaction
Consent of two-thirds of unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
A maximum limit specified in the placement memorandum by the Manager

payload.explanation: Reg. 17(c): leverage or borrowing is subject to consent from the investors and to a maximum limit as may be specified by the Board. Transaction-by-transaction approval and the two-thirds-by-value test belong to other provisions.

answer.explanation: Reg. 17(c): leverage or borrowing is subject to consent from the investors and to a maximum limit as may be specified by the Board. Transaction-by-transaction approval and the two-thirds-by-value test belong to other provisions.

activities.title: On what two conditions may a Category III AIF employ leverage?

payload.q: On what two conditions may a Category III AIF employ leverage?
payload.answer: Consent from the investors in the fund, and a maximum limit as may be specified by the Board — with periodic disclosure of overall leverage, leverage from cash borrowing, leverage from derivatives or complex products, and the main source, to investors and to the Board.

activities.title: Valuation: independent valuer, but the Manager owns the outcome

payload.hook: The regulation splits valuation into two responsibilities that are easy to conflate: who performs it, and who is answerable for it.

cards.title: An independent valuer
cards.law: The Manager shall ensure that the Alternative Investment Fund appoints an independent valuer who satisfies the criteria specified by the Board from time to time.
cards.means: Appointment of an independent valuer is mandatory, on criteria the Board specifies.
cards.watch: An internal committee does not satisfy this.

cards.title: The Manager, for true and fair value
cards.law: The Manager shall be responsible for true and fair valuation of the investments of the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund.
cards.means: Delegating the computation does not transfer responsibility for the result.
cards.watch: An independent valuer's report is not a defence to an unfair valuation.

cards.title: Depart, document, report
cards.law: Provided that in case the established policies and procedures of valuation do not result in fair and appropriate valuation, the Manager shall deviate from the established policies and procedures in order to value the assets at a fair value and document the rationale for such deviation: Provided further that such deviation and its rationale shall be reported to the trustee or the trustee company or the Board of Directors or designated partners and investors.
cards.means: Where policy produces an unfair result, the Manager must depart from it, document why, and report the departure.
cards.watch: Deviation is mandatory in that situation, not discretionary — 'shall deviate'.

payload.summary: The Manager must ensure an independent valuer meeting the Board's criteria is appointed and that valuation is carried out as specified, while remaining responsible for true and fair valuation; where established policies would not produce a fair value the Manager shall deviate, document the rationale, and report the deviation and its rationale to the trustee, board or designated partners and to investors.
payload.tip: Build the deviation trail before you need it: a dated rationale and a record of the report to the trustee and investors. The provision is drafted as an obligation to depart from policy, so silence when policy misprices is itself the breach.

activities.title: Where established valuation policies would not produce a fair and appr

payload.q: Where established valuation policies would not produce a fair and appropriate valuation, the Manager:

options.t: May continue applying the policy, provided the limitation is disclosed to investors
Shall deviate from the policy, document the rationale, and report the deviation
Must obtain the Board's prior approval before departing from the stated policy
Shall refer the valuation to the trustee, whose determination is then final

payload.explanation: The provisos to Reg. 23 make deviation mandatory in that situation ('shall deviate'), coupled with documentation of the rationale and reporting of the deviation and its rationale to the trustee, board or designated partners and to investors.

answer.explanation: The provisos to Reg. 23 make deviation mandatory in that situation ('shall deviate'), coupled with documentation of the rationale and reporting of the deviation and its rationale to the trustee, board or designated partners and to investors.

activities.title: An AIF appoints an independent valuer who computes the portfolio value

payload.q: An AIF appoints an independent valuer who computes the portfolio value. Responsibility for true and fair valuation:

options.t: Passes to the independent valuer once the appointment has been made
Is shared between the Manager and the trustee in equal measure
Remains with the Manager, notwithstanding the valuer's appointment
Rests with the trustee, who must countersign the valuation report

payload.explanation: The Manager must ensure an independent valuer is appointed, but Reg. 23 separately makes the Manager responsible for true and fair valuation. Appointing a valuer discharges the appointment duty, not the responsibility for the outcome.

answer.explanation: The Manager must ensure an independent valuer is appointed, but Reg. 23 separately makes the Manager responsible for true and fair valuation. Appointing a valuer discharges the appointment duty, not the responsibility for the outcome.

activities.title: Three categories, one registration slot

payload.hook: An AIF does not choose a category as a label; it registers in exactly one, and the category fixes what it may invest in, whether it may leverage, and whether it may be open-ended. Put a fund in the wrong slot and every downstream condition is wrong.

cards.title: The 'positive spillover' box
cards.law: Category I funds invest in start-ups, early-stage ventures, social ventures, SMEs, infrastructure or other sectors the Board or Government considers socially or economically desirable, and include venture capital funds, SME Funds, angel funds, social impact funds, infrastructure funds and special situation funds.
cards.means: Category I is defined by where it invests and the incentive rationale behind it — not by strategy sophistication. It is a family of named sub-categories, not a single fund type.
cards.watch: Angel funds are a Category I sub-category (inserted 09-09-2025); special situation funds were added earlier (24-01-2022). Older material that lists only VCF/SME/social/infra is out of date.
cards.link: Sub-category selection drives the investment conditions in Chapter 8.

cards.title: The residual box
cards.law: A Category II AIF is one that does not fall in Category I or III and does not undertake leverage or borrowing other than as permitted in these regulations; private equity funds and debt funds for which no specific incentives are given are included.
cards.means: Category II is a residual definition — you land here by not being I or III. Its hallmark is the absence of a leverage strategy, not any positive investment mandate.
cards.watch: 'Does not undertake leverage or borrowing other than as permitted' — the permitted 30-day operational borrowing does not push a fund out of Category II.
cards.link: The permitted borrowing carve-out is drilled in Chapter 8.

cards.title: The only leverage box
cards.law: A Category III AIF employs diverse or complex trading strategies and may employ leverage, including through investment in listed or unlisted derivatives; hedge funds and funds trading for short-term returns are included, and such funds may be open-ended.
cards.means: Category III is the only category defined by permission to leverage as a strategy. It is also the natural home for open-ended, short-horizon funds.
cards.watch: Leverage as a strategy is a Category III marker. A Category I/II fund that merely borrows short-term for operations has not become Category III.
cards.link: Category III's leverage cap and disclosure were covered in Chapter 4.

payload.summary: One registration slot fixes everything: Category I is the named-sub-category, incentive-driven box (VCF, SME, angel, social impact, infrastructure, special situation); Category II is the residual, no-strategic-leverage box (PE, debt); Category III is the only strategic-leverage box (hedge, short-term, may be open-ended).
payload.tip: When a fund's strategy is ambiguous, decide leverage first: strategic leverage forces Category III; its absence, plus no Category I incentive mandate, lands you in Category II by residual definition. Getting the slot right at registration is cheaper than a material-change filing later.

activities.title: Who the Board lets through the gate

payload.hook: Registration is not a formality. Before a certificate issues, the constitutive documents, the people, and the plan must each clear a named test. Miss one and the application is not deficient — it is ineligible.

cards.title: The documents must permit the activity
cards.law: The memorandum, trust deed or partnership deed must permit the applicant to carry on AIF activity and must prohibit it from inviting the public to subscribe; a trust deed must be registered under the Registration Act, 1908 and an LLP deed filed under the LLP Act, 2008.
cards.means: The fund's own charter has to authorise the business and forbid a public offer. Private placement is baked in at the constitution, not bolted on later.
cards.watch: 'Prohibited from inviting the public' is an eligibility condition, not merely an operating rule — a permissive deed fails Reg. 4(b).
cards.link: Private placement is why the PPM regime (Chapter 9), not a prospectus, governs.

cards.title: The people are tested by an external yardstick
cards.law: The applicant, Sponsor and Manager must be fit and proper persons based on the criteria in Schedule II of the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008.
cards.means: Fit-and-proper is not judged on an AIF-specific scale; it borrows the Intermediaries Regulations standard, covering integrity, competence, financial soundness and record.
cards.watch: The test attaches to three parties — applicant, Sponsor AND Manager. A clean Manager does not cure a tainted Sponsor.
cards.link: The same persons carry the fiduciary duty in Chapter 11.

cards.title: Certification plus qualification
cards.law: The Manager's key investment team must have at least one key personnel with the relevant certification specified by the Board and at least one with a professional qualification in finance, accountancy, business management, commerce, economics, capital market or banking (or a CFA charter); the same person may satisfy both, and fresh certification must be obtained before the existing one expires.
cards.means: The competence gate is now certification-and-qualification, and one qualified, certified person can satisfy both limbs — but the certification must be kept live.
cards.watch: This replaced the old 'five years' experience' test. Answering from the pre-2020/2023 experience rule is a dated-material error.
cards.link: The shift is tracked in Chapter 14.

cards.title: Describe the fund, or fail Reg. 4(i)
cards.law: The applicant must clearly describe, at registration, the investment objective, targeted investors, proposed corpus, investment style or strategy and proposed tenure of the fund or scheme.
cards.means: A vague application is an ineligible application. The regulator wants the fund's shape stated up front, because category, corpus and tenure all flow from it.
cards.watch: Whether the applicant or any Sponsor/Manager entity was earlier refused registration is itself a listed consideration under Reg. 4(j).
cards.link: The stated corpus meets the minimum-corpus gate from Chapter 1.

payload.summary: Eligibility (Reg. 4) is four gates: a constitution that permits AIF activity and forbids a public invitation (trust registered, LLP filed); applicant, Sponsor and Manager all fit and proper on the Intermediaries-Regulations yardstick; a key team meeting the certification-plus-qualification test kept continuously live; and a clearly described objective, investors, corpus, strategy and tenure. The certificate, once granted under a specific category, is valid until the AIF is wound up.
payload.tip: Run eligibility as a checklist across three parties, not one. The most common rejection driver is not the numbers — it is a deed that permits a public invitation, or a Sponsor who fails fit-and-proper while the Manager is clean.

activities.title: The limits that bind every rupee deployed

payload.hook: Category tells you what a fund is; the investment conditions tell you what it may actually do with the money — how much in one company, whether it may borrow, and how idle cash may sit. These are the rules an inspector reconciles against the portfolio.

cards.title: 25% for I and II, 10% for III
cards.law: Category I and Category II AIFs shall invest not more than twenty-five per cent of investable funds in one investee company; Category III AIFs shall invest not more than ten per cent, with large value funds for accredited investors permitted up to twenty per cent.
cards.means: The single-name cap is tighter for Category III (10%) than for I and II (25%), reflecting Category III's trading character; LVFs get a relaxation to 20%.
cards.watch: The number flips by category. Applying 25% to a Category III fund, or 10% to a Category II fund, is the classic concentration error.
cards.link: The LVF relaxations recur across corpus, PPM and concentration.

cards.title: 30 days, 4 times, 10%
cards.law: Category I and Category II AIFs shall not borrow or leverage for making investments, except to meet temporary funding and day-to-day operational requirements for not more than thirty days, on not more than four occasions in a year, and not more than ten per cent of investable funds.
cards.means: The borrowing carve-out is a narrow operational bridge, fenced by three simultaneous limits — duration, frequency and size — every one of which must hold.
cards.watch: All three limits are cumulative. A 35-day bridge, or a fifth occasion, or 11% of investable funds each independently breaches Reg. 16(1)(c)/17(c).
cards.link: Using this bridge as investment leverage is what pushes a fund into Category III territory (Chapter 6).

cards.title: The venture mandate has a floor
cards.law: At least seventy-five per cent of the investable funds of a venture capital fund shall be invested in unlisted equity shares or equity-linked instruments of a venture capital undertaking, or in companies listed or proposed to be listed on an SME exchange, to be achieved by the end of the fund's life cycle.
cards.means: A VCF cannot drift into being a generalist fund — three-quarters of its money is mandated toward genuine venture and SME exposure, tested over the whole life cycle.
cards.watch: The 75% is measured 'by the end of the life cycle', not at every point in time — an early portfolio below 75% is not automatically in breach.
cards.link: This sub-category floor sits on top of the Category I conditions from Chapter 6.

cards.title: Investments in demat, idle cash parked
cards.law: AIFs shall hold their investments in dematerialised form subject to specified conditions; un-invested investable funds and divestment proceeds pending distribution may be parked in liquid mutual funds, bank deposits or high-quality liquid assets such as Treasury bills, TREPS, commercial papers and certificates of deposit.
cards.means: Two housekeeping rules: portfolio holdings go demat (with narrow carve-outs), and idle money must sit in defined liquid instruments, not be deployed off-mandate.
cards.watch: The demat holding rule (inserted 05-01-2024) is separate from the demat issuance of the fund's own units — do not conflate the two.
cards.link: Dematerialisation is developed in Chapter 12.

payload.summary: Investment conditions bind every deployment: single-company concentration is 25% for Category I and II and 10% for Category III (20% for Category III LVFs); operational borrowing is permitted only within all three limits at once — 30 days, 4 occasions a year, 10% of investable funds; a VCF must reach 75% in unlisted/SME-listed venture exposure by end of life cycle; and holdings sit in demat with idle cash confined to defined liquid instruments.
payload.tip: When you audit a portfolio, test the borrowing carve-out on all three axes at once — practitioners breach it on frequency (a fifth draw) far more often than on the headline 30 days. And always confirm which concentration number applies before you measure a position; the category, not the position size, tells you the cap.

activities.title: How a scheme actually gets to launch

payload.hook: A scheme is not born when the manager decides to raise money; it is born when a compliant placement memorandum is filed and the launch clock is satisfied. The 2026 GARUDA change rewired that clock — the old wait-for-comments model is gone.

cards.title: The disclosure document, defined
cards.law: The placement memorandum shall disclose investment strategy, risk-management tools, key service providers, the terms of reference of the approving committee, conflicts of interest and the procedures to address them, disciplinary history, the terms on which the Manager offers services, affiliations, and the manner of winding up — all that an investor needs to take an informed decision.
cards.means: The PPM is the AIF's prospectus-equivalent for a private-placement world: it is where strategy, conflicts and exit are disclosed once, in a Board-specified template.
cards.watch: Because the fund is barred from public invitation, the PPM — not a public prospectus — is the governing offer document. Conflicts disclosure is a listed mandatory head, not optional colour.
cards.link: The conflicts duty is enforced through Chapter 11.

cards.title: Through a merchant banker, before launch
cards.law: Schemes may be launched subject to filing the placement memorandum with the Board through a merchant banker at least thirty days prior to launch, with fees under the Second Schedule; the first scheme is exempt from scheme fees, and large value funds for accredited investors are exempt from the filing and comment requirements.
cards.means: Routine schemes route the PPM through a merchant banker who has done independent diligence; the first scheme pays no scheme fee; LVFs skip the filing-and-comment machinery altogether.
cards.watch: Scheme-fee exemption is only for the first scheme — not every scheme. LVF exemption is from the filing/comment step, not from having a PPM.
cards.link: The LVF light-touch runs through corpus, tenure and PPM alike.

cards.title: Rollout upon acknowledgement
cards.law: Under the GARUDA green channel (Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement, effective 30 July 2026), an AIF may proceed to launch its regular scheme after ten working days of filing the placement memorandum through a merchant banker who has independently exercised due diligence of the disclosures.
cards.means: GARUDA replaces waiting for SEBI's prior comments with a merchant-banker-diligenced, acknowledgement-based launch after a short working-day window. Speed shifts to the market, accountability shifts to the merchant banker and Manager.
cards.watch: GARUDA is a Master Circular mechanism dated 30-07-2026 — cite it as a circular, never as a regulation. The Manager and merchant banker, not SEBI's silence, carry responsibility for accuracy.
cards.link: Tracked as a 2026 change in Chapter 14.

cards.title: 12 months, and the tenure clock
cards.law: The first close of a scheme shall be declared not later than twelve months from the date the AIF becomes eligible to launch it; the corpus at first close shall not be below the minimum for the category; and the tenure of a close-ended scheme is calculated from the date of first close. If first close is not declared in time, a fresh application and fee are required.
cards.means: First close is the anchor date — it must land within twelve months, must clear the minimum corpus, and it starts the tenure clock. Miss it and you re-file.
cards.watch: Tenure runs from FIRST close, not final close (except legacy schemes that had declared first close by 17-11-2022). Miss the twelve-month window and the scheme must be re-applied for.
cards.link: Tenure and extension were covered in Chapter 2; this is where the clock starts.

payload.summary: A scheme reaches launch through the PPM regime: a Board-template placement memorandum disclosing strategy, conflicts and exit, filed through a merchant banker at least thirty days before launch (first scheme fee-exempt; LVFs exempt from filing/comment). Under GARUDA (30-07-2026) launch follows ten working days after a merchant-banker-diligenced filing rather than awaiting SEBI comments. First close must be declared within twelve months, at or above minimum corpus, and starts the close-ended tenure clock.
payload.tip: Diary the first-close date the moment a scheme is filed — it is the single date that both proves timely launch and starts tenure. Under GARUDA the merchant banker's independent diligence is now the control that used to be SEBI's comment letter; keep that diligence file, because responsibility for PPM accuracy sits with the Manager and merchant banker.

cards.title: Two crore, or seven-and-a-half, or the split test

cards.means: Three alternative routes to individual accreditation — a pure income route, a pure net-worth route, and a combined route with a lower income if net worth backs it up.
cards.watch: The value of the primary residence is excluded from net worth. The three limbs are alternatives — meeting any one qualifies.
cards.link: Accreditation drives the ticket carve-out in Chapter 1 and the LVF regime throughout.

cards.title: Fifty crore for the institutions
cards.law: Trusts other than family trusts, and body corporates, qualify as accredited investors with net worth of at least fifty crore rupees; partnership firms qualify where each partner independently meets the criteria.
cards.means: For institutional forms the single test is a fifty-crore net worth; a partnership must clear it partner-by-partner rather than in aggregate.
cards.watch: Do not carry the individual figures across to entities — the trust/body-corporate threshold is a flat fifty crore, not the seven-and-a-half-crore individual number.

cards.title: Come direct, pay no distribution fee
cards.law: Schemes of AIFs shall offer investors a Direct Plan, which shall not carry any distribution or placement fee, and investors who approach the AIF directly without a distributor shall be onboarded through the Direct Plan only.
cards.means: An investor who arrives without an intermediary must not be charged distribution economics — the Direct Plan strips the placement fee out entirely.

cards.title: A ring-fenced side-car for accredited investors

activities.title: The standing duties between the raise and the exit

payload.hook: Once money is in, the fund runs on standing duties: a fiduciary standard, conflict management, transparency, and periodic reporting. And a governance twist — the people who sit on the investment committee carry the Manager's liability with them.

cards.title: Sponsor and Manager owe the investors
cards.law: The Sponsor and Manager of an AIF shall act in a fiduciary capacity towards the fund's investors, shall disclose all conflicts of interest as and when they arise, and shall monitor and appropriately mitigate conflicts of interest throughout the scope of business.
cards.means: The relationship is fiduciary, not merely contractual — the Sponsor and Manager must put investors first, surface conflicts as they arise, and actively manage them, not just disclose once.
cards.watch: The duty is continuous ('as and when they arise', 'throughout the scope of business') — a one-time PPM disclosure does not discharge it.
cards.link: The conflicts first disclosed in the PPM (Chapter 9) must be managed here.

cards.title: Disclosure is a standing obligation
cards.law: All AIFs shall ensure transparency and disclosure of information to investors, including on financial and material information, fees and charges, and any inquiry or legal action, in the manner specified.
cards.means: Transparency is codified, not cultural: material information, the fee stack and any regulatory action must reach investors as a matter of obligation.
cards.watch: Transparency runs to investors continuously; it is distinct from the periodic reporting the fund owes SEBI.
cards.link: Investor-facing transparency pairs with the SI-Portal reporting below.

cards.title: Sit on the IC, share the liability
cards.law: A Manager may constitute an investment committee to approve investment decisions; the members of such an investment committee shall be equally responsible as the Manager for the fund's investment decisions and for compliance with the regulations.
cards.means: The IC is not an advisory fig leaf. Whoever approves the deals is placed on the same liability footing as the Manager — external members included.
cards.watch: External IC members do not dilute liability; they share it. This is the trap for funds that treat the IC as an outside advisory panel.
cards.link: Liability for default flows through to Chapter 13.

cards.title: SI Portal and the annual CTR
cards.law: AIFs shall file periodic reports on the SEBI Intermediary Portal within the specified calendar-day timelines, and shall submit a Compliance Test Report within thirty days from the end of the financial year, with the trustee or sponsor intimating observations to the manager within thirty days and changes made within fifteen days.
cards.means: Two reporting rhythms: routine activity reporting to the SI Portal on tight day-counts, and an annual compliance self-test (CTR) with a defined review-and-cure loop.
cards.watch: The CTR is annual, from the end of the financial year, with a 30-day file / 30-day intimate / 15-day cure cycle — distinct from the SI-Portal periodic filings.
cards.link: Reporting discipline is what an inspection (Chapter 13) tests first.

payload.summary: The operating phase runs on standing duties: a fiduciary standard on Sponsor and Manager with continuous conflict disclosure and mitigation; codified transparency to investors on material information and fees; an investment committee whose members bear liability equally with the Manager; and periodic reporting to the SEBI Intermediary Portal plus an annual Compliance Test Report on a 30-day file, 30-day intimate, 15-day cure cycle.
payload.tip: Treat the investment committee's liability as the sharpest governance point: if external members approve deals, paper their role, their diligence and their access to information, because the regulator places them on the Manager's liability footing. And run the CTR as a genuine annual self-audit — it is the document an inspector reads before anything else.

activities.title: The plumbing that protects the investor

payload.hook: Behind the strategy sits the investor-protection plumbing: units held in demat, portfolios valued by an arms-length independent valuer, and every investor holding pari-passu unless they have specifically stepped out. It is unglamorous — and it is exactly what an inspection reconciles.

cards.title: Units and holdings, in demat
cards.law: AIFs shall issue their units in dematerialised form, and schemes above the specified corpus threshold (corpus greater than five hundred crore rupees as on the reference date) were brought into mandatory demat crediting on a phased timeline; investors' units are credited to their demat accounts.
cards.means: Dematerialisation runs on two levels — the fund issues units in demat, and larger funds were phased into mandatory demat crediting first by a corpus threshold.
cards.watch: The five-hundred-crore corpus threshold sequenced the roll-out; it is not a permanent exemption for smaller funds, which follow on the later timeline.
cards.link: Demat holding of the portfolio was flagged in Chapter 8.

cards.title: Arms-length, qualified, tested
cards.law: An AIF shall value its investments through an independent valuer who is not an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee, who has at least three years' experience in valuation, and who is registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India as a valuer or is a holding company or subsidiary of a credit rating agency; valuation follows the endorsed IPEV guidelines.
cards.means: Valuation independence is defined structurally — no associate relationship — and by qualification: three years' experience plus an IBBI registration or CRA-group status, applying the IPEV standard.
cards.watch: 'Not an associate of the manager, sponsor or trustee' is the core independence test; an in-house or affiliated valuer fails it however qualified.
cards.link: The Manager's non-delegable responsibility for valuation was covered in Chapter 5.

cards.title: 20% flags a material change
cards.law: Where there is a deviation of more than twenty per cent between two consecutive valuations of an asset, or a change in the valuation methodology or approach, the manager shall report it to investors with the reasons, as specified.
cards.means: A large valuation swing or a methodology change is treated as material and must be surfaced to investors — it cannot be smoothed over silently.
cards.watch: The 20% trigger is asset-level and between consecutive valuations; a methodology change triggers reporting independently of the percentage.
cards.link: Materiality and disclosure connect back to Chapter 11 transparency.

cards.title: Equal rights, with named exceptions
cards.law: Investors shall have rights pro-rata to their commitment in each investment and pari-passu in all respects; the pro-rata requirement does not apply where an investor is excused or excluded from a particular investment or has defaulted on a capital call, and differential rights may be offered only without affecting others' pari-passu and pro-rata rights (carried interest excepted).
cards.means: The default is equality — pro-rata by commitment, pari-passu in rights — broken only in named, principled cases: excuse/exclusion, default, or carried interest.
cards.watch: Differential rights are not freely negotiable; they are permitted only where they do not erode other investors' pari-passu and pro-rata position. Excuse/exclusion and default are the recognised pro-rata exceptions.
cards.link: Ring-fencing and equal rights also govern the CIV schemes of Chapter 10.

payload.summary: The investor-protection layer: units issued in demat, with larger funds (corpus above five hundred crore) phased into mandatory demat crediting first; portfolios valued by an independent valuer who is not an associate of manager/sponsor/trustee, has three years' experience and IBBI registration or CRA-group status, applying IPEV; deviations above twenty per cent between consecutive valuations or any methodology change reported to investors; and investors holding pro-rata to commitment and pari-passu, with excuse/exclusion, default and carried interest as the only recognised departures.
payload.tip: When you review a valuation policy, test independence before competence — an affiliated valuer fails the associate test no matter how qualified. activities.title: How a fund is examined, and how it ends

payload.hook: Supervision and exit are the bookend of the lifecycle. SEBI can look in without warning; a fund that fails the rules is dealt with under the Intermediaries machinery; and when a fund's life runs out, there is a defined path through liquidation, dissolution and — new in 2026 — 'Inoperative Fund' status.

cards.title: Suo motu, and notice can be waived
cards.law: The Board may, suo motu or on information or complaint, appoint an Inspecting Authority to examine an AIF's books, records and documents; it shall ordinarily give not less than ten days' notice, but may, where satisfied it is in investors' interest, order inspection without notice.
cards.means: Inspection needs no wrongdoing to begin, and while ten days' notice is the norm, the regulator can dispense with notice entirely where investors' interest demands it.
cards.watch: 'Not less than ten days' notice' is the default, not a guarantee — the no-notice override under Reg. 31(2) is a live power.
cards.link: The cooperation duty makes the inspection workable; see below.

cards.title: Everyone connected must assist
cards.law: Every officer of the AIF and any associated person in possession of relevant information, including the manager, must produce books, accounts and documents, furnish information and extend all cooperation to the Inspecting Authority, which may examine persons on oath and take authenticated copies.
cards.means: The duty to assist reaches beyond the compliance desk to every officer and associated person — and the Inspecting Authority can put them on oath.
cards.watch: The obligation is not confined to the compliance officer; withholding by any connected person is itself a default.
cards.link: Non-cooperation is a listed default trigger below.

cards.title: Dealt with under the Intermediaries route
cards.law: An AIF that contravenes the Act or regulations, furnishes false or misleading information, fails to submit returns, does not cooperate in an inspection, or fails to resolve investor complaints shall be dealt with under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, without prejudice to the Board's directions under Reg. 34 or its powers under sections 11, 11B, 11D and related provisions.
cards.means: Enforcement is not free-standing — it is channelled through the Intermediaries Regulations, layered on top of the Board's direction and Section-11 powers.
cards.watch: Non-cooperation in an inspection and failure to resolve investor complaints are themselves default triggers, not merely procedural lapses.
cards.link: Post-inspection, Reg. 34 lets the Board bar new schemes, freeze assets or order refunds.

cards.title: Retention capped, and a 2026 status
cards.law: A trust-form AIF is wound up on expiry of tenure, on a resolution of at least seventy-five per cent of investors by value, or where the Board so directs; unliquidated investments may be distributed in-specie or taken into a dissolution period with seventy-five per cent investor approval; retention of proceeds beyond permissible fund life shall not exceed three years, and a fund may apply to SEBI for 'Inoperative Fund' status (Master Circular, 2026).
cards.means: Exit has structure: a 75%-by-value investor vote or tenure expiry or a Board direction ends the fund; leftovers go in-specie or into a dissolution period; and proceeds can be held only up to three years beyond fund life, after which 'Inoperative Fund' status is the parking bay.
cards.watch: The winding-up and dissolution-period investor thresholds are seventy-five per cent by value; the three-year retention cap and 'Inoperative Fund' status are 2026 circular additions — cite them as circular, not regulation.
cards.link: The 2026 additions are tracked in Chapter 14.

payload.summary: Supervision and exit: SEBI may inspect suo motu with ten days' notice as the norm but a no-notice override in investors' interest, and every officer and associated person must cooperate, on oath if required; a defaulting AIF is dealt with under the SEBI (Intermediaries) Regulations, 2008, with non-cooperation and unresolved complaints as named triggers, and post-inspection directions under Reg. 34; winding up follows tenure expiry, a seventy-five-per-cent-by-value vote or a Board direction, with unliquidated assets going in-specie or into a dissolution period (seventy-five per cent approval), retention capped at three years beyond fund life, and 'Inoperative Fund' status available under the 2026 circular.
payload.tip: Build a standing inspection file — books, CTRs, valuation policy, investor registers — because the ten-day notice can be waived, and the cooperation duty binds every officer, not just compliance. On exit, hold the two seventy-five-per-cent-by-value thresholds and the three-year retention cap precisely; they are the numbers a winding-up plan is judged against.

activities.title: What changed, when, and from which source

payload.hook: Mastery of the AIF regime is partly a mastery of dates. The last three years reshaped categories, borrowing, dematerialisation and exit — and the two most recent moves, GARUDA and the Inoperative Fund, live in the circular, not the regulation. Knowing which is which is the whole game.

cards.title: The operational carve-out and demat holdings
cards.law: The Fourth Amendment, 2024 (w.e.f. 07-08-2024) recast the Category I and II borrowing carve-out to cover temporary funding and day-to-day operational requirements within 30 days / 4 occasions / 10%; and the requirement to hold investments in dematerialised form was inserted (w.e.f. 05-01-2024).
cards.means: 2024 tightened and clarified the borrowing bridge and pushed the portfolio itself into demat — two operational changes with real audit consequences.
cards.watch: The 2024 borrowing change is to the carve-out wording; it did not create a new leverage freedom. Demat holding of the portfolio is distinct from demat issuance of units.
cards.link: Both are drilled in Chapter 8.

cards.title: A new Category I sub-category
cards.law: The Second Amendment, 2025 (w.e.f. 09-09-2025) brought angel funds expressly within the list of Category I sub-categories in Reg. 3(4), moving them from the earlier standalone Chapter III-A treatment.
cards.means: Angel funds were formally folded into the Category I family — older material treating them as a separate chapter-based construct is out of date.
cards.watch: Angel funds are now a Category I sub-category; listing Category I without them is a dated answer.
cards.link: The current sub-category list is in Chapter 6.

cards.title: The green-channel launch mechanism
cards.law: The GARUDA circular (Green-Channel: AIF Rollout Upon Document Acknowledgement), dated 30 July 2026, allows a regular scheme to launch after ten working days of a merchant-banker-diligenced PPM filing, replacing the wait-for-prior-comments model.
cards.means: GARUDA is the 2026 speed-up of scheme launch, with accountability resting on the merchant banker's independent diligence and the Manager.
cards.watch: GARUDA is a Master Circular mechanism (30-07-2026) — never cite it as a regulation. It changes the launch clock, not the PPM's contents.
cards.link: The launch mechanism is in Chapter 9.

cards.title: Retention capped, a new parking status
cards.law: The June 2026 winding-up circular caps retention of proceeds at three years beyond permissible fund life and introduces 'Inoperative Fund' status, for which an AIF applies to SEBI; the dissolution-period and in-specie routes for unliquidated investments carry a seventy-five-per-cent-by-value investor threshold.
cards.means: 2026 gave the end-of-life a clean architecture: a three-year retention ceiling and an 'Inoperative Fund' parking status, sitting alongside the dissolution-period mechanics.
cards.watch: Retention cap and 'Inoperative Fund' status are circular, dated 2026 — cite them as circular provisions. The exit vote is seventy-five per cent by value.
cards.link: The exit mechanics are in Chapter 13.

payload.summary: The recent reshaping, by date and source: 2024 recast the Category I/II operational borrowing carve-out (07-08-2024) and required demat holding of investments (05-01-2024); 2025 folded angel funds into the Category I sub-categories (09-09-2025); and 2026 delivered two circular-level changes — GARUDA green-channel launch (30-07-2026) and the winding-up circular's three-year retention cap plus 'Inoperative Fund' status. Regulation changes are cited to the amendment regulations; GARUDA and Inoperative Fund are cited to the Master Circular.

In an inspection or an opinion, the fastest way to lose credibility is to attribute a 2026 circular mechanism like GARUDA or 'Inoperative Fund' to the Regulations; the source label is part of the answer.
